James K. Polk. The eleventh President of the United States, serving from eighteen forty-five to eighteen forty-nine in a single term marked by aggressive territorial expansion and the Mexican-American War. A staunch advocate of Manifest Destiny, Polk orchestrated the acquisition of vast western territories including present-day California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and New Mexico. His presidency represented the apex of American expansionism in the nineteenth century and set the stage for sectional conflict over slavery in the newly acquired lands. Polk was elected in eighteen forty-four as a "dark horse" candidate on a platform of territorial expansion and aggressive nationalism, defeating Henry Clay, who opposed Manifest Destiny, with the rallying cry "Fifty-Four Forty or Fight!" regarding Oregon territory. He campaigned for the annexation of Texas, independent since eighteen thirty-six, and exclusive American control of Oregon, claimed by both the United States and Britain, pledging to extend American territory to the Pacific Ocean in all directions. Polk successfully annexed Texas in eighteen forty-five, precipitating Mexican hostility and setting conditions for war. Mexico viewed Texas as a rebellious province and considered American annexation an act of aggression justifying military response. He led the nation through the Mexican-American War from eighteen forty-six to eighteen forty-eight, personally directing strategy despite lacking military experience. American forces under Generals Zachary Taylor and Winfield Scott advanced deep into Mexico, capturing Mexico City itself. Polk acquired over five hundred twenty-five thousand square miles of territory through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in eighteen forty-eight, nearly doubling American territorial extent. Mexico received fifteen million dollars in compensation but lost half its national territory, including present-day California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, and most of New Mexico. He settled the Oregon boundary dispute with Britain diplomatically in eighteen forty-six, establishing the forty-ninth parallel as the U.S.-Canada border in the Pacific Northwest, abandoning the "Fifty-Four Forty or Fight!" slogan when cooler heads prevailed. Polk promised to serve only one term and kept that promise, declining nomination in eighteen forty-eight despite significant popularity during his presidency. He maintained he sought only to accomplish his expansionist goals and then retire, though some historians argue he exhausted himself and his presidency.
